A '''similarity system of triangles''' is a specific configuration involving a set of triangles.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Mauldon|first=J.G.|date=May 1966|title=Similar Triangles|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=39|issue=3|pages=165–174|doi=10.1080/0025570X.1966.11975709}}</ref> A set of triangles is considered a [[Configuration (geometry)|configuration]] when all of the triangles share a minimum of one incidence relation with one of the other triangles present in the set.<ref name=":0" /> An [[Incidence (geometry)|incidence relation]] between triangles refers to when two triangles share a point. For example, the two triangles to the right, <math>AHC</math> and <math>BHC</math>, are a configuration made up of two incident relations, since points <math>C</math>and <math>H</math>are shared. The triangles that make up configurations are known as component triangles.<ref name=":0" /> Triangles must not only be a part of a configuration set to be in a similarity system, but must also be directly similar.<ref name=":0" /> Direct similarity implies that all angles are equal between two given triangle and that they share the same rotational sense.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Similar.html|title=Similar|last=Weisstein|first=Eric|website=Wolfram MathWorld|access-date=2018-12-12}}</ref> As is seen in the adjacent images, in the directly similar triangles, the rotation of <math>B</math> onto  <math>C</math> and <math>B^1</math>  onto  <math>C^1</math>occurs in the same direction. In the opposite similar triangles, the rotation of <math>B</math> onto  <math>C</math> and <math>B^1</math> onto  <math>C^1</math> occurs in the opposite direction. In sum, a configuration is a similarity system when all triangles in the set, lie in the same plane and the following holds true: if there are ''n'' triangles in the set and ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 triangles are directly similar, then n triangles are directly similar.<ref name=":0" />

== Background ==
J.G. Mauldon introduced the idea of similarity systems of triangles in his paper in <u>Mathematics Magazine</u> "Similar Triangles".<ref name=":0" /> Mauldon began his analyses by examining given triangles <math>ABC, XYZ</math> for direct similarity through complex numbers, specifically the equation <math>\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ x & y & z \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0</math>.<ref name=":0" /> He then furthered his analyses to equilateral triangles, showing that if a triangle <math>ABC</math> satisfied the equation <math>a + wb + w^2c =0</math> when <math>w = \frac{-1 + i\surd3}{2}</math>, it was equilateral.<ref name=":0" /> As evidence of this work, he applied his conjectures on direct similarity and equilateral triangles in proving [[Napoleon's theorem]].<ref name=":0" /> He then built off Napoleon by proving that if an [[equilateral triangle]] was constructed with equilateral triangles incident on each vertex, the midpoints of the connecting lines between the non-incident vertices of the outer three equilateral triangles create an equilateral triangle.<ref name=":0" /> Other similar work was done by the French Geometer [[Victor Thébault|Thébault]] in his proof that given a [[parallelogram]] and squares that lie on each side of the parallelogram, the centers of the squares create a square.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Gerber|first=Leon|date=October 1980|title=Napoleon's Theorem and the Parallelogram Inequality for Affine-Regular Polygons|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=87|issue=8|pages=644–648|jstor=2320952|doi=10.1080/00029890.1980.11995110}}</ref> Mauldon then analyzed coplanar sets of triangles, determining if they were similarity systems based on the criterion, if all but one of the triangles were directly similar, then all of the triangles are directly similar.<ref name=":0" />

== Examples ==
=== Triangles appended to a rectangle ===
==== Direct similarity ====
If we construct a rectangle <math>ABCD</math> with directly similar triangles <math>PAB, QBC, RCD, SDA</math> on each side of the rectangle that are similar to <math>PQS</math>, then <math>RQS</math> is directly similar and the set of triangles <math>\{PAB, QBC, RCD, SDA, PQS, RQS\}</math> is a similarity system.<ref name=":0" />

==== Indirect similarity ====
However, if we acknowledge that the triangles can be degenerate and take points <math>B</math> and <math>P</math> to lie on each other and <math>Q, R, D</math>and  <math>S</math> to lie on each other, then the set of triangles is no longer a direct similarity system since the second triangle has area and the others do not.<ref name=":0" />

=== Rectangular parallelepiped ===
Given a figure where three sets of lines are parallel, but not equivalent in length (formally known as a rectangular [[parallelepiped]]) with all points of order two being labelled as follows:

<math display="block">\{A_1B_1C_1, A_2B_2C_2, A_3B_3C_3, A_4B_4C_4, A_1B_4C_3, A_2B_3C_4, A_3B_2C_1, A_4B_1C_2\}</math>

Then we can take the above points, analyze them as triangles and we can show that they form a similarity system.<ref name=":0" />

''Proof:''

In order for any given triangle, <math>KLM</math>, to be directly similar to <math>A_1, B_1, C_1</math>the following equation should be satisfied:

: <math>(\ell-m)a_1+ (m-k)b_1+(k-1)c_1=0.</math><ref name=":0" />   where ''ℓ'', ''m'', ''k'', ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>1</sub>, and ''c''<sub>1</sub> are sides of triangles.

If the same pattern is followed for the rest of the triangles, one will notice that the summation of the equations for the first four triangles and the summation of the equations for the last four triangles provides the same result.<ref name=":0" /> Therefore, by the definition of a similarity system of triangles, no matter the seven similar triangles selected, the eighth will satisfy the system, making them all directly similar.<ref name=":0" />
